surfaces.part: wall top / coping band (brown tile pattern)
rounded stone end pier on left with snow patches

answer.evidence: In the column at x=24, rows 2-9 show a brown patterned band with dark dashes, which reads as a sloped coping or tile plane. Row 10 is a light edge line (L=200), and row 11 is a dark eave shadow (L=111) with darker notches in rows 11-12. Below that, the brick front face runs from row 12 to row 47 with mortar courses, so the front face is about 37 rows. The rounded stone end on the left is drawn as a profile of stacked stones. It has no isometric receding side face. The overall structure is a top band over a tall south face, which matches the 'cabinet: top + edge + eave' reference.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a small stone wall-end piece (grey stone blocks with a rounded, tower-like end cap). It is not a whole building with roof, walls and door/windows, so it does not match the reference kind. Its measured tones per tile (19) are above the references (12 and 10), and near-flat coverage is only 3%, so density by the numbers is not the problem. The outline is the issue: 100% of the dark edge pixels are neutral, against 7% and 9% for the references, and the picture shows a dark grey/black line around the blocks and end cap. This is the uniform near-black 'sticker' look rather than a dark tone of the adjacent material. The stone ramp has about 4 steps (white highlight, light grey, mid grey, dark grey), fewer than the roof and wall ramps of the references at 5-6. Blocks are rendered with some texture, but the shading is more uniform than the reference stones, which are shaded one by one. The neutral outline and shallower ramp make it fall short of the Beodeul standard.

surfaces.part: top band of wall (brown tile/coping strip)
snow cap on left stone corner pillar

answer.evidence: The wall has a brown patterned band in rows 1-9 across the top. A light front-edge line sits at row 10, and dark shadow notches follow in rows 11-13, so the band reads as a horizontal top surface. Below it, rows 11-47 hold a tall south face of stone bricks. The rounded stone corner on the left carries snow and is drawn as a vertical rubble face, which is acceptable for a wall end. The whole object is a front face with a top band above it, so it reads as three-quarter.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a small wall-end piece: a grey stone wall segment with a rounded, curled end cap. The references are whole buildings with roofs, doors and windows, so the kind does not match well and the comparison is only partial. Measured facts: 19 visible tones per tile, above the references' 12 and 10, with 3% near-flat coverage, so density by the numbers is fine. But 100% of dark edge pixels are neutral, against 7% and 9% for the references, so the outline is a neutral near-black line. That is the sticker look, while the references use tinted dark material tones. The stone ramp shows about 4 grey steps, compared with 5-6 in the references. The brick courses have some texture, but the curled end reads as a flat grey and white fill with a heavy dark outline. The neutral outline is the deciding weakness.
